newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia leaders feud, predict end to Khmer Rouge.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia leaders feud, predict end to Khmer Rouge.

text.p: Despised Khmer Rouge strongman Pol Pot was reported to be heading for Thailand on Monday after most of his remaining fighters deserted him, with Cambodia's government split over its policy toward the rebels.

First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said on Monday that Pol Pot, reported to be on the run after slaughtering his defence chief and 11 family members, had fled toward the Thai border on Sunday in a convoy of 10 trucks.
He said six of the trucks were caught by Khmer Rouge guerrillas who had broken with their leader, the mastermind of Cambodia's 1975-79 "killing fields" reign of terror.
Thailand closed that part of the border last week and pledged to help Cambodia capture Pol Pot.
"This is the end of the Khmer Rouge...," Ranariddh said, speaking at a pagoda inauguration west of Phnom Penh.
He predicted Pol Pot's hard-liners would be captured within two days.

Ranariddh appeared to be heading for a showdown with his co-Prime Minister Hun Sen over how to handle the disintegration of the guerrilla movement after Hun Sen warned that government officials who negotiated with the Khmer Rouge should be arrested.
The co-premiers' conflicting agendas and the problem of contradictory reports prompted representatives of the two leaders' parties to meet on Monday to discuss the best way to handle the situation.

After the meeting, committee representative and co-Minister of Interior Sar Keng told reporters Ranariddh's announcement on Monday that hard-line rebels from the guerrilla base of Anlong Veng would join the government seemed premature.
"It seems to be fast. It cannot be done," he said.
There were six divisions ready to defect in Anlong Veng and two more that remain loyal to Pol Pot, but the government needed more information on the intentions of both groups, Sar Kheng said.
Ranariddh had said about 95 percent of the guerrillas from Anlong Veng and a division led by Pol Pot, including four unnamed top officials, had decided to join the government.
Pol Pot was reported on Friday to have fled Anlong Veng after the guerrilla movement, already decimated by thousands of defections last August, split over whether to make peace with Phnom Penh.
The guerrillas reneged on a 1991 peace pact meant to end Cambodia's long history of conflict and have been fighting the coalition government formed after a U.N.-sponsored poll in May 1993.

Pol Pot was still holding senior figures as hostages, including Khieu Samphan, president of the Khmer Rouge's provisional government, Ranariddh said on Monday. Rebel commander Ta Mok had broken with Pol Pot and disappeared, he said.
He said Briton Christopher Howes, abducted in March 1996 in Cambodia's northwest, was also in the group but could not say whether the British mine clearance expert was alive.
None of the reports about what is happening around Anlong Veng have been independently confirmed.
Many analysts wonder whether the entire episode may have been cooked up to distance the totally unpalatable Pol Pot from his marginally less despised comrades, who harbour some political aspirations.

In a surprise revelation, Ranariddh said he had met Khieu Samphan and two of his associates three weeks ago, but refused to provide details. Khieu Samphan recently said he hopes to form a political alliance with Ranariddh, a prospect the prince has welcomed.
The news of secret talks did not sit well with Hun Sen.
In a speech on local radio, he warned anyone who negotiated with Khieu Samphan or other top rebels was breaking Cambodian law and would face arrest.
He demanded the Khmer Rouge leaders be arrested and brought to trial.

"Khieu Samphan has been supporting Pol Pot from the very beginning to the very end, so there is no way to stage any negotiations with Khieu Samphan, but now there have been negotiations with Khieu Samphan, which is illegal...," he said.
Relations between Ranariddh and Hun Sen, forced into an unhappy alliance by the U.N. elections in 1993, have deteriorated ahead of new polls due in 1998.
Hun Sen said he suspected a conspiracy to allow the rebels to enter politics.
"The Khmer Rouge is dead militarily, but someone wants the Khmer Rouge to survive politically. No way," Hun Sen said.
Hun Sen was part of the Vietnamese invasion force that eventually overthrew the Khmer Rouge regime and later led the Hanoi-backed government that ruled until 1991.
More than one million Cambodians died during the Khmer Rouge's disastrous experiment in total communism through executions, starvation, disease and hard labour.
